We use cookies to enhance your browsing experience, serve personalized ads or content, and analyze our traffic. By clicking "Accept All", you consent to our use of cookies.

We use cookies to help you navigate efficiently and perform certain functions. You will find detailed information about all cookies under each consent category below.

The cookies that are categorized as "Necessary" are stored on your browser as they are essential for enabling the basic functionalities of the site. ...Show more

Necessary cookies are required to enable the basic features of this site, such as providing secure log-in or adjusting your consent preferences. These cookies do not store any personally identifiable data.

Functional cookies help perform certain functionalities like sharing the content of the website on social media platforms, collecting feedback, and other third-party features.

Analytical cookies are used to understand how visitors interact with the website. These cookies help provide information on metrics such as the number of visitors, bounce rate, traffic source, etc.

Performance cookies are used to understand and analyze the key performance indexes of the website which helps in delivering a better user experience for the visitors.

Advertisement cookies are used to provide visitors with customized advertisements based on the pages you visited previously and to analyze the effectiveness of the ad campaigns.

_**Bankers and advisers involved in Apollo Global Management’s £5.7bn acquisition of easyJet are expected to receive approximately £334m in fees, making the transaction one of the UK’s most lucrative takeovers for dealmakers this year, according to a report by the Financial Times.**_

Apollo will pay approximately £280m in fees, including £190m associated with arranging acquisition financing, while easyJet will pay a further £54m.

Advisers to Apollo include Barclays, PJT Partners, Citigroup and law firm Paul Weiss, while easyJet’s advisers include Evercore, BNP Paribas, Panmure Liberum and Clifford Chance.

Apollo secured the acquisition after outbidding rival private credit manager Castlelake, which had previously been in negotiations with the airline.

The transaction will take easyJet private after more than two decades on the stock market, with Apollo planning to reposition the business towards higher-value travel and improve its financial performance.

The proposed ownership structure has also been revised to comply with EU aviation regulations requiring majority European ownership and control.

Under the revised arrangements, easyJet’s board will reportedly comprise of 10 directors, including four Apollo representatives and two appointed by existing shareholders.

Founder Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou is expected to transfer his family’s existing 15% holding into the private company, giving the family a stake of between 45.1% and 49.9%.
